title: Basil's new city
hook: Basil of Caesarea built a place of care for the poor and sick, and his friend called it a new city

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pachomius' community, and your line was together is harder, and better. Which chore did you share, and did you stay until it was done? Day seven hundred seventy-three.

"I will pull down my barns, and build greater." That's the rich man in one of Jesus' parables, in Luke's Gospel. His harvest is huge, so he plans bigger storage, and that night his life is asked of him. A man named Basil, then a priest in Caesarea, in what's now central Turkey, and later its bishop, preached on that line to his own people. And in his time, a famine came to his city. The rich of the city, like the man in the parable, had full barns. Basil had a sermon, a pulpit, and a gift for making people uncomfortable. What he did with them is today's story, and by the end he's built something on the edge of town that his close friend would call a new city.

The famine comes first. His friend Gregory tells it, in a speech in Basil's memory. Basil opened the storehouses of those who had them, by the force of his preaching. He gathered the hungry in one place, and he didn't just organize it. He served them himself, with his own hands, alongside his helpers. In his sermon on the barns, Basil pushes hard. In paraphrase: the bread you keep in store belongs to the hungry; the coat in your closet belongs to the one without one. He isn't asking for leftovers. He's asking whose the extra really is. Then he builds. Outside Caesarea, Basil put up a whole complex: lodging for travelers and strangers, a place for the poor, care for the sick, with people to nurse them and workers to keep it going. A local governor was apparently uneasy about it. Basil wrote to him: what harm does this do the state? We're housing strangers and caring for the sick. Gregory's speech describes it with real wonder. Go a little way out of the city, he says in paraphrase, and look at the new city, a storehouse of devotion, where the rich put their surplus. And he singles out the people others avoided: those with the disease that disfigured skin and drove sufferers out of town. Basil, Gregory says, didn't keep his distance. He greeted them, embraced them, even kissed them, as brothers. That's the image to keep. Not a building, but a bishop bending down to kiss someone everyone else had sent away. A city of mercy, built just outside the city.
screen: `THE FAMINE: HE SERVED WITH HIS HANDS.`
`THE BREAD YOU KEEP IS THE HUNGRY'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a place near you where people are cared for when they're sick or poor. A hospital, a free clinic, a hospice, a shelter, a food bank. If you've ever been carried by one, remember that. Picture the people who work there tonight, in the late hours. Basil asked his governor what harm the place did. Ask the opposite: what does this place run short of? Blankets, cans, a driver, a thank-you for the night staff. Choose one small gift you could actually give it. If you pray, you can pray for the people inside, the sick and the ones who care for them. The bell holds the time.
Basil's new city. The place of care Basil of Caesarea built outside his town, for strangers, the poor and the sick, that his friend Gregory called a new city.
Your line: a city of mercy. Today, give the gift you chose to a hospital, clinic, shelter or food bank, even if it's small. Day seven hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Churches and Christian orders run hospitals, clinics, hospices, shelters and food banks, and church members give to and volunteer in them.

fork.setup: you're Basil. a governor is uneasy about your new buildings outside town. what do you do?
options: tear them down to keep the peace.
write to him: what harm does it do to house strangers and nurse the sick?
fork.reveal: Basil wrote to defend it, describing the lodging for strangers and the care for the sick.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bishop is someone who runs services and meetings.
what it means: Basil built a place outside his city for strangers, the poor and the sick, and nursed them himself.
what a scholar hears: Gregory of Nazianzus' funeral speech for Basil, Oration 43, and Basil's own letter defending the buildings.

notes: The index hook says 'one of the first hospitals for the poor and sick'; per the claims rule the script and hook avoid 'first'. Confirm, or restore the index hook.
Famine relief: Gregory, Oration 43.35–36 (opened storehouses by preaching, gathered the hungry, served with his own hands). Paraphrased; confirm.

The line 'the bread you keep belongs to the hungry; the coat ... belongs to the one without one' is paraphrased from Basil's homily; confirm which homily it belongs to (Homily on Luke 12:18 or the homily 'To the Rich').
Letter 94 to the governor Elias defending the buildings: paraphrased; confirm the governor's unease and details.

Oration 43.63: 'go forth a little from the city and behold the new city, the storehouse of piety'; and Basil greeting and kissing those with leprosy. Paraphrased; confirm. The script avoids the word 'leper'.
The hook does not claim the barns sermon came before or during the famine; some date it to the famine. Confirm.

Editor pass: 'his best friend' (superlative) became 'his close friend'; varied the stock 'start with' teach opener; the practice now draws on Basil's own question instead of repeating day 764's 'money, time or hands' list.

Second editor pass: 'who gave the speech at Basil's funeral' became 'in a speech in Basil's memory'. Oration 43 is traditionally called the funeral oration but is usually thought to have been delivered some time after Basil's death, not at the funeral; the script no longer places it there.

Audit pass: FACT FIX. The hook called Basil a bishop at the time of the famine; Gregory (Oration 43.34–36) places the famine while Basil was still a presbyter (he became bishop in 370). Hook now says 'then a priest ... and later its bishop'. Practice no longer repeats day 765's give-away-from-your-closet practice; it now asks what the place of care runs short of.
